about: Our own sightings, made with the sky view from a known spot. Unlike data/labels.json (public reports matched to the pinned snapshot), each entry here records what was measured, so it can test direction, height, and timing, not only whether a plume was seen. Add one entry per launch watched, including launches where nothing was seen.

fields.seen: none, rocket (a moving point of light), or plume (a wide sunlit cloud).
fields.points: Rocket positions read from sky view screenshots: seconds after liftoff (from the screenshot time), azimuth and elevation in degrees read from the drawn grid, about +/-2 degrees.
fields.model: What the engine gave for the same seconds after liftoff, as a range over the profile members.
fields.compassCheck: The drawn Sun against the real Sun from the same spot, before recalibrating. Tells whether a direction error was the phone compass.

observations.modelProfiles: The model values above use the falcon9-leo members of 2026-10-13 (SpaceX CRS-16 and CRS-14, 2018). For the 2020 members added on 2026-10-15, run node scripts/compare-ascent-sources.js.

compassCheck.result: Drawn Sun ring on the real Sun within about 1 degree, before recalibrating, with the stored correction. Same spot as the SpX-35 viewing (Ben). Phone held level, after the roll fix. Facing west (Sun at 250), while SpX-35 was viewed facing southeast; compass error near metal can change with heading, so a check facing southeast would close this fully.

observations.note: Height and timing agree within about 1 degree. Rocket 19 to 29 degrees farther east than the engine at the same moments; it sat on or just under the drawn arc. The 2026-10-15 compass check found the compass right within about 1 degree, so a compass error of 20 degrees is unlikely; the old code's roll error was about 1 degree per degree of roll, and the SpX-35 screenshots show only 2 to 3 degrees of roll. Leading explanation: the real ascent ran farther downrange at those times than the 2018 profiles.
